To address this issue, a decision feedback equalizer was initially applied with satisfactory results, however its effectiveness was impeded due to the occurrence of burst errors resulting from unpredictable marine conditions. Networks (TCNs) hold great promise for handling time-series data. TCNs leverage a technique called time-dilated convolution that poses an optimization challenge which typically demands significant experimentation. We've developed a technique to automate the dilation optimization process by casting it as a weight-pruning operation along the time axis. Our method learns dilation factors concurrently with weights during training and achieves notable gains in model compactness and inference efficiency without compromising accuracy. It produces a range of highly optimal TCN variants from a single starting model, surpassing the performance of custom-designed networks in both efficiency and accuracy. Our approach also facilitates the exploration of numerous model configurations with minimal experimentation required, and we've made our code and data available at the specified URL. Experimental evaluations on four signal-level and 19 dataset-level experiments across various application domains reveal our method's ability to yield efficient and accurate models. These models have already been deployed in real-world industrial settings, highlighting the practicality of our approach. Our technique serves as a precursor to further dilation optimization frameworks, as it assumes weights are optimized through common deep learning techniques such as batch normalization and retraining. As such, it is viable as a preprocessing step to enhance weights prior to further compression or pruning. With minor modifications, our method can also be applied to other convolutional neural networks beyond TCNs, opening up possibilities for efficient inference in additional domains. Literature can be broadly categorized into two main areas based on whether intermediate cues are employed: direct methods and two-stage pipelines. In the latter category, CNN regresses intermediate cues such as object coordinates or virtual control points instead of pose parameters in the initial stage. Object pose is then resolved through the construction of correspondence constraints utilizing these intermediate cues. This study concentrates on refining two-stage pipelines by combining two distinct concepts: projection grouping on one hand and correspondence learning on the other. We initially employ a patch-based method to forecast projection heatmaps, representing the likelihood distribution of projected corners from 3D bounding boxes. Next, a correspondence network is utilized to generate correspondences between projections and images. Finally, a perspective-n-point (PnP) algorithm is applied for object pose estimation utilizing correspondences and 3D bounding box centers. Our experiments demonstrate notable enhancements over state-of-the-art methods on diverse datasets, notably the Lie group regression (LGR) benchmark of the EUV dataset and moderate challenges of the PASCAL 3D+ dataset. In silicon material, T-type damage centers have shown significant potential for this interface, thanks to their unique optical properties in the O-band region and long-lived electronic and nuclear spin lifetimes. Although research on these defect centers has so far been conducted as part of bulk silicon studies, we demonstrate the consistent creation of high T center densities within the 220nm device layer of Silicon-On-Insulator (SOI) wafers, using a process that combines ion implantation and heat treatment. By developing a method to measure spin-dependent optical transitions, we found that high T center densities within the active layer of photonic integrated devices can be achieved by optimizing both the implantation energy and heat treatment temperature. As a result, we were able to create functional optomechanical devices with high T center densities, offering promising possibilities for scalable quantum technology applications. However, above a certain threshold (approximately 8.85 x 10^48 erg s) the boundaries broke into two distinct branches, resulting from objects losing mass and experiencing extreme spin. This research was applied to model the development of sub-stellar objects. Two possible scenarios were modeled: one with external forces gradually slowing the star, mainly controlled by spin-down time, and another where the star spins out of control, ultimately shedding mass and shrinking. In the case of sustained nuclear reactions, spin-down time had the greatest impact, causing the boundary of 10.8 x 10^48 erg s. For objects that lose mass due to spinning, a smaller angular momentum threshold (approximately 8.85 x 10^48 erg s) leads to further breakdown at approximately 8.54 x 10^48 erg s. These revised angular momentum limits are more restrictive and thus more conservative estimates for the stable hydrogen burning of very low-mass stars. This research also highlights the potential for objects on the edge of sustainable nuclear energy to be stabilized through external applied centrifugal force. Computer

It can be demonstrated that any knot diagram can be converted into a trivial unknot through a sequence of unknotting operations, combined with some variations in the diagram configuration, which are referred to as Reidemeister moves. Unknotting operations hold significant value in the field of knot theory; they serve a purpose in analyzing the process of untangling knots and may also have implications for untangling processes in other complex systems. Thus far, research has focused on identifying distinct unknotting steps from a given knot diagram, but the order in which these steps occur is not fixed and can vary greatly. This paper presents a new approach where the time it takes to untangle a knot is measured not by the number of unknotting operations, but by the longest sequence of moves required to release a single crossing. This new approach leads to the creation of a new metric, termed the $k$-length of a knot, with the property that it increases with the number of knots and may provide a new perspective on understanding the complexity of untangling knots. This model is then applied to study the time it takes to untangle knots in three-dimensional space and the results show a similar growth pattern, but at a slower rate, when compared to the volume of the knot space. Additionally, the paper presents a new universal bound that applies to all knots, derived from the $k$-length metric, which may have implications for developing untangling algorithms with better performance.

increasing interest in the Intelligent Reflecting Surface (IRS) technology. Comprised of passive reflective components that can modulate the characteristics of incoming waveforms, such as phase, amplitude, frequency, and polarization, an IRS offers a means to actively control the characteristics of wireless channels. Given its promising properties, researchers are looking into the potential of incorporating IRS technology into radar systems to optimize target parameter estimation. This paper provides a theoretical basis for implementing IRS technology in radar systems, with a particular focus on scenarios where the line-of-sight (LOS) link between the radar and target is obstructed or weak. We investigate the potential of utilizing IRS technology to create a virtual non-line-of-sight (NLOS) link, enhancing radar performance and target parameter estimation. Through numerical simulations and comparative analyses under both optimized and non-optimized scenarios, we demonstrate the effectiveness of the IRS-provided virtual link in target parameter estimation when the LOS link strength is lower than a relative strength of $~10^{-1}$ in comparison to the NLOS link. This paper also publishes the related source code. Moreover, we propose the VCA-2D algorithm to allocate reflective coefficients across two dimensions and the VCA-3D algorithm to allocate them across three dimensions, both of which exhibit improved performance in target parameter estimation. This research paves the way for further exploration of IRS technology's potential in radar systems, with particular emphasis on its ability to create virtual links that could potentially be applied in scenarios with multiple targets.

ysics is the common envelope (CE) phase of binary star evolution, where two stars are enveloped in the shedding material from one of them. This process triggers a shrinking of the orbit as the stars interact with the envelope. Ultimately, it can result in either mergers or further complex interactions, which can involve a mix of compact objects and stars. Certain CE scenarios, particularly those involving white dwarfs, can produce supernovae, while neutron star mergers can result in gamma-ray bursts, and all types of compact object mergers can produce gravitational waves. Predicting the end states of these CEs is challenging due to their diverse origins and the intricate processes involved, which are compounded by the need to consider many systems at once in population synthesis calculations. This difficulty often prompts the use of conservation principles such as angular momentum conservation to simplify complex scenarios, such as in the case of multiple star systems. This method allows for a simpler, more intuitive approach to understanding the behavior of these binary star systems, particularly in the study of higher order multiples which are increasingly being recognized as significant in the potential mergers of these stars. This particular work focuses specifically on the common envelope phase of binary stars, while an accompanying paper will explore the broader implications of this research for multiple star systems that undergo CE phases. This paper first begins by outlining the various models used to predict the outcomes of CEs, before examining conservation of angular momentum in these scenarios, and finally exploring conservation of linear and orbital momentum in greater detail.

Researchers have a rich history of developing and analyzing preservation-based discretization techniques, including validating existing schemes' preservation properties and proposing innovative methods achieving both high accuracy and property preservation. Although such schemes, when paired with implicit time-stepping methods, ensure preservation of certain properties, they are generally limited by requiring an exact solution to the nonlinear system of equations for each time-step. To address this limitation, this study proposes modifying the flexible generalised minimum residual iteration to enforce constraints on numerical approximations, and demonstrates its applicability to both conservative and dissipative systems. Specifically, two model problems - the time-dependent plane elastic problem and the time-dependent Stokes problem - are used to illustrate the method's efficiency and effectiveness. The proposed enforcement strategy exhibits comparable computational performance to the original iterative solver for systems without constraints, and demonstrates robustness in handling both under-determined and over-determined systems. To further confirm the method's efficacy, extensive numerical experiments are performed, and the results indicate that it retains the same accuracy and stability as the corresponding free systems. As the proposed method flagrantly disregards traditional numerical analysis principles, a heuristic justification is provided to ensure integrity. Finally, the paper's findings are discussed in the broader context of structured iterative solvers, and areas are identified for possible future enhancement

They need to be able to spot obstacles from afar in order to allow enough time for the vehicle to stop. Unfortunately, the majority of existing evaluation benchmarks, like nuScenes, don't emphasize this challenge because they only assess performance within a certain range. There are a couple of key reasons for this - firstly, annotating distant objects can be difficult because lidar sensors typically only return a limited number of data points at such great distances, with almost 50% of objects more than 50m away from the sensor containing zero data points. Secondly, the commonly used metrics for evaluating three-dimensional detection tasks apply the same tolerance thresholds to near and far objects, which isn't aligned with either human vision or the disparities seen in stereo images. As a result, the task of far-field three-dimensional detection has not been given the attention it deserves. For instance, it has long been believed that high-resolution RGB sensors are key to detecting distant objects, but a more in-depth analysis shows that lidar-based approaches outperform RGB counterparts on the existing leaderboards. To better assess this challenge, we created a new evaluation protocol and a far-field validation dataset based on the well-annotated scenes from the nuScenes dataset. We compared a variety of three-dimensional detection methods with this protocol and the results verify the widely-held assumption that high-resolution RGB does enhance detection in the far field; nonetheless, these improvements are quite costly

Deep neural network-based classifiers have a common issue, however - they often provide predictions that seem excessively certain but do not reflect the true likelihood of classification accuracy. This limitation is attributed to the inherent closed-world nature of traditional softmax formulation. As cross-entropy loss encourages models to classify inputs into a fixed number of pre-defined categories, this can result in overly confident predictions that fail to capture true uncertainty. To address this shortcoming, a novel $K$+1-way softmax formulation is proposed. This approach involves introducing an extra dimension to account for uncertainty and proposes an innovative energy-based objective function to unify both classification tasks and uncertainty modeling. Furthermore, theoretical analysis reveals that optimizing this function effectively captures the marginal data distribution in the uncertainty dimension. Our experiments demonstrate that Energy-based Deep Network-based methods produce highly reliable and confident predictions with minimal risk, surpassing current state-of-the-art techniques in robustness and confidence calibration. This improvement is shown across multiple benchmark datasets and evaluation metrics, highlighting the superior robustness and confidence calibration of Energy-based Deep Network-based models. This advancement is particularly significant as it paves the way for evaluating the generalization ability of machine learning models in both inference and training phases with a focus on modeling uncertainty correctly. This idea is further developed as a preprocessing technique, called uncertainty normalization. This simple yet efficient method successfully improves the confidence calibration of any pre-trained classifier. All the code is available at: https://github.com/aleksandrkondoloft/EDN

During training, we discovered that the relationship proposal distribution is skewed, with the majority of incorrect relationships being easily identified due to poor object detection. As a result, low-frequency difficult proposals struggle to contribute effectively. Our proposed framework, Spatially-Aware Balanced Negative Proposal Sampling (SABRA), mitigates the impact of false positives in VRD tasks. To counter the imbalance, SABRA incorporates Balanced Negative Proposal Sampling (BNPS), which divides proposals into distinct sub-classes based on difficulty and samples a balanced distribution accordingly. A previously developed approach by Baker achieved PTAS on various graph classes including planar graphs. Further, Romero, Wrochna, and Zivny developed a simpler PTAS for certain graph classes using the Sherali-Adams LP relaxation for maximum CSPs with constraints defined by arbitrary non-negative functions.

This research is extended to CSPs with constraints that have multiple possible values. The only restriction for such constraints is that they contain an element that is at least as acceptable as all other elements.

A new PTAS is presented for general-valued CSPs with constraints that have distinct values, such as 0 and 1, but with specific limitations. The technique was previously applicable to classes where Baker's approach worked, except possibly fractionally-treewidth-fragile classes. The findings relax the monotonicity condition of the constraints, allowing a new property called diagonalisability. This property includes treewidth, chordal structure, and the good-neighbor property. The research also shows that all diagrammatically definable constraints are diagonalisable. The new PTAS uses a more complex iteration of the Sherali-Adams LP relaxation with new inequalities derived from the original CSP instance. Current methods of weather prediction, using either a network of sensors or a vehicle-mounted camera, are limited in scope and costly.
A robust weather detection system is crucial for seamless operation of transportation services in diverse weather conditions.
However, this task is complex due to the varied nature of weather and the scarcity of distinct characteristics that distinguish different weather conditions.
Existing approaches to this problem are largely confined to specific environments and only tackle the classification of two weather types.
In this study, we introduce the RFS dataset, which includes images representing three categories of weather (rain, snow, and fog), and propose a novel algorithm utilizing super-pixel masks for data augmentation to yield satisfactory results using multiple Convolutional Neural Network configurations.

This article aims to enhance the definition of angle function to accommodate spaces with the property of betweenness, which it deems a more fundamental framework. Within this revised framework, the article provides solutions to Menger's initially posed problems. This article also introduces the term 'homogeneous space with an angle function' and investigates its properties in the context of finite-dimensional Euclidean spaces. This investigation includes the identification of spaces with an angle function that are homothetic to certain standard Euclidean spaces, as well as the classification of spaces with an angle function that are homothetic to the standard Euclidean plane.

To overcome these limitations, we present a new approach to evaluating defensive strategies in team sports, using machine learning to classify game scenarios into three categories, based on previous rulebook analysis, and demonstrate this approach's effectiveness in predicting contract renewals for football coaches and odds to win a championship from a team. By comparing our models to those of a leading sports data analyst, we confirm our innovative method's feasibility with minimal additional data, yielding comparable performance at essentially no extra cost. This advancement opens up possibilities for similar evaluations of offensive strategies and comprehensive team performance, enabling data-driven decision-making for sports managers and a promising source of valuable business insights with minimal data requirements. Additionally, our code and data are available for reproduction and further exploration, offering opportunities for statisticians and sports enthusiasts to build upon this work. Furthermore, we explore ways to apply this approach to other team sports with minimal modifications. Ultimately, our research paves the way for streamlined and cost-effective evaluation of sports teams' performance in diverse scenarios.

a model from distributed data on a graph is a challenging task, especially when it comes to Federated Learning. A significant obstacle in this process is the substantial communication required between nodes and the server. A common strategy used to address this issue involves each node making several local model updates before sharing the updated model with the server. Although this method reduces communication costs, it introduces statistical disparities among the nodes' data sets, leading to slower model convergence and biases. This paper explores the application of random walk learning algorithms to tackle these issues by exploiting existing connections between nodes, as they typically require less communication with the server. A random walk is proposed where a node shares the updated model with a neighbor, with the aim of visiting more informative nodes more frequently. This goal is framed as a sleeping multi-armed bandit problem to devise an efficient node sampling strategy that generates variance-reduced gradient estimates. A novel adaptive random walk learning algorithm is introduced and proven to converge theoretically. Moreover, our results demonstrate its superior performance compared to other random walk algorithms. This work also includes a node eligibility threshold strategy to optimize communication costs, as well as a data plasticity graph framework to address changing network topologies. Our experiments validate the algorithms' effectiveness across various datasets and graphs. This work is accompanied by an open-source code repository to facilitate future research and implementation. An analysis of North Carolina court cases between 1994 and 2009 examined how court-ordered mental health treatment as part of probation affects an offender's chances of returning to the justice system.  The research focuses on offenders who were sentenced to probation and assesses those who were required to undergo mental health treatment against those who were not.  It discovered that receiving mental health treatment as part of their sentence lowered the odds of recidivism within a three-year time frame by 17 percent or 5.6 percentage points. An initial financial analysis of these results indicates the decrease in future crime could cover and exceed the expenses associated with providing treatment.  To understand these findings, a literature review is presented to highlight prior research's related findings. It is essential to note that these findings may not be generalizable due to data limitations and potential selection bias issues. When we extend a raft made of particles by expanding its surface of support, we see that its breaking pattern changes constantly based on the rate at which we are stretching it. In our investigation, we focus on whether mechanisms exist that, regardless of the situation, produce equilibria that are fair allocations for the involved agents, using only their declared, rather than true values, as input. Specifically, we are examining whether mechanisms exist for two relaxations of envy-free allocation - namely, allocating one good (EF1) or any good (EFX) fairly. Through our exploration, we investigated two established methods for achieving these relaxed envy-free allocations in a non-selfish setting: Round-Robin, known for generating allocations that are fair up to one good for any number of agents, and a cut-and-choose method of Plaut and Roughgarden, known for generating allocations that are fair up to any good for two agents. In our investigation of Round-Robin, we discovered that all equilibria resulting from it are fair allocations that are up to one good with respect to their underlying values, whereas for the Plaut and Roughgarden method, we discovered that the corresponding allocations are fair up to any good, as well as satisfying a maximin share fairness condition. Moreover, we established that for any mechanism with two agents that always has an equilibrium producing an EFX allocation, this allocation is in fact a fair up-to-any-good allocation, though this does not apply to mechanisms with more than two agents.

This difficulty arises from not only the random fluctuations inherent to noisy data but also limitations imposed by data quantity, model specifications, hyperparameters, optimization techniques, sampling, and overfitting. Despite some recent efforts to quantify uncertainty within neural networks, no overarching framework effectively addresses uncertainty quantification even in relatively simple cases such as function approximation. netting has far-reaching effects on a nation's economy, affecting transactions and business-to-business interactions. Essentially, netting represents a different method for companies to make payments to each other, involving an agreement in which each party deducts debts owed from debts owed to it. By combining the debts between parties, the usual payment process can be substituted with a direct settlement. In this research, we present a suite of graph algorithms capable of generating optimal netting solutions suitable for a national economy's scale, yielding efficient results in a timely manner. Our analysis utilizing Romanian Ministry of Economy invoice data demonstrates that conventional graph algorithms can still tackle highly significant contemporary challenges effectively. Furthermore, we identify areas for enhancing current research in this domain. This study also introduces the NIST Standard Reference Model for Payment System Optimization, which involves a payment system's graph algorithm as a key component. Ultimately, our research is also applicable to other multi-party settlement scenarios. One such scenario is the European Central Bank's target sector of cross-border trade, which poses particular computational challenges due to the lack of comprehensive invoice data from participating nations. Despite this difficulty, our results obtained using a combination of actual and artificially generated Romanian invoice data indicate that conventional graph algorithms can still yield optimal or near-optimal solutions in a timely manner. This is further confirmed by performance metrics obtained from artificially generated data mimicking the structure of the Romanian invoice data. These results indicate that the payment system's processing time remains acceptably low even as the number of participating companies increases.

Despite this limitation, a range of applications, including real-world programs with inherent object structures, have been overlooked for parallelization opportunities.  Our research identified a particular subset of object-oriented programming called Single-Method Multiple-Objects (SMMO), which can be efficiently parallelized on SIMD devices by executing the same method across multiple objects of a given type.  To facilitate easy adoption of high-speed GPU programming for average developers, we created the DynaSOAr CUDA framework specifically tailored for SMMO applications.  This framework includes a dynamic memory allocator that is both lock-free and parallel, a data layout domain-specific language (DSL), and a do-all operation that is both parallel and efficient.  As a result, DynaSOAr offers improved memory usage, reduced fragmentation, and superior performance to leading state-of-the-art GPU memory allocators by concurrently managing both memory allocation and memory access through atomic operations.  Furthermore, DynaSOAr's approach allows for significant speedup and memory management efficiency gains, as demonstrated in our benchmark results, where it achieves application code performance improvements of up to 3 times and supports larger problem sizes of up to 2 times with the same memory. This feature provides a physical justification for adopting a specific covariant harmonic gauge that arises when a mass term is added to the gravitational perturbation.  Specifically, one particular choice of harmonic gauge leads to a linearized massive gravity model with the correct five degrees of freedom and avoids the vDVZ discontinuity, in contrast to the standard Fierz-Pauli theory.  This analysis also reveals that this new model is equivalent to the linearized massive gravity proposed by Cheng, Feng, and Li, but using a harmonic gauge framework provides an alternative and more natural proof of the theory's consistency.  Furthermore, this approach can potentially address the issue of parameter dependence that may arise in the new model.  The discussion is extended to include a linearized massive graviton in the harmonic gauge framework, and the resulting theory is shown to be free from vDVZ discontinuity.  The stability of the theory is analyzed using the tree-level scattering amplitude of two gravitons, and the appearance of a flat potential in the scattering process suggests that the new model may resolve the little hierarchy problem.  The interpretation of the additional degree of freedom as a pseudo-Nambu-Goldstone boson is also explored, and the relevance of this concept is connected to the mechanism of spontaneous symmetry breaking of the de Sitter space through a linear dilaton metric.

For domains with irregular boundaries, using a grid without a set pattern to calculate the potential by splitting it into small areas becomes impractical due to high computational costs. In this paper, we propose an efficient and straightforward high-order method for calculating Newtonian potentials based on Green's identity, which simplifies the complex volume integration into boundary integrals. Our new method makes expensive computations of near field interactions on an unstructured grid comparable to the time it takes for far field interactions.
